power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Patients within the neurodivergent spectrum, high-ability profiles, and other high processing cost phenotypes (HPCPh) frequently present a clinical paradox: marked cognitive domains alongside debilitating functional collapse, burnout, dysautonomia, and migrating multisystem symptoms.
Standard cross-sectional laboratory investigations against population references routinely prove inconclusive or trigger fragmented, iatrogenic interventions.

Here, we define the Third Allostasis: an evolutionarily conserved biophysical regime wherein the organism displaces peripheral homeostasis and lowers systemic throughput to defend central nervous system membrane viability when environmental and informational demands approach the kinetic limits of transmembrane ion clearance.

Through within-person longitudinal follow-up of five adult HPCPh trajectories-spanning stepped recovery from decade-long containment, live entry into acute biological helplessness, endothelial-natriuretic decompression, cognitive restoration, and exit from chronic matrix dysautonomia-we demonstrate how this regime becomes clinically visible using four routine laboratory instruments.

We introduce accessible arithmetic tools for any consulting room: the red-cell hydration index (Ht -3 × Hb) and two "Rules of Three" (OsmP@290 and Na@290) that unmask hidden plasma osmolal gaps driven by uncharged organic osmolytes, even when raw osmolality and sodium remain within normal limits.

Crucially, while an open osmolal gap signals fast-axis intercompartmental shift, clinical direction requires "whole-column reading" across slower coupled buffers, including circadian cortisol, tissue thyroid gating (FT3/rT3), iron-ferritin dynamics, prolactin, and monocytes.

Recognizing the Third Allostasis shifts clinical practice from treating isolated organ abnormalities to reading the organism's adaptive effort as a whole, guiding contextual adjustments that relieve central overload and restore functional vitality.

The model presented here emerged progressively from naturalistic clinical follow-up: systematic observation and long-term tracking of clinical and laboratory profiles in patients who did not respond to standard protocols, nor fitted easily into any single diagnostic label.

In prior work we have described them as high processing cost phenotypes (HPCPh), a transdiagnostic perspective that reconnects neurodevelopmental trajectories and atypical presentations with developmental biology, systems neuroscience and allostatic physiology 1, 2 .
text.formatted: In prior work we have described them as high processing cost phenotypes (HPCPh), a transdiagnostic perspective that reconnects neurodevelopmental trajectories and atypical presentations with developmental biology, systems neuroscience and allostatic physiology <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> .

text.text: These patients commonly show a clinical paradox: marked high-performance domains alongside impaired day-to-day functioning, with clinical patterns that span depression-like states, burnout, dysautonomia and migrating multisystem symptoms (skin, gut, muscle, autonomic, vestibular) that leave investigations inconclusive 3, 4 .
text.formatted: These patients commonly show a clinical paradox: marked high-performance domains alongside impaired day-to-day functioning, with clinical patterns that span depression-like states, burnout, dysautonomia and migrating multisystem symptoms (skin, gut, muscle, autonomic, vestibular) that leave investigations inconclusive <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> .

text.text: Many are currently classified within the neurodivergent spectrum: autism, ADHD, twice-exceptionality, high ability and giftedness, with or without learning disabilities.

The challenge of understanding the multiple systems involved and the diversity of clinical presentations has always been accompanied by the perception of common features pointing towards a connection that explains clinical and laboratory presentations across the cases.

Two findings organize the common ground in these cases: an intense, rapid and atypical biological response to changes in the nature or intensity of informational load, and the regression of symptoms and laboratory parameters when the external context was adjusted to each patient's architecture.

Organizing those parameters longitudinally, and reading them within the person, revealed an allostatic multisystem dynamic that is completely missed when laboratory results are read one by one, against population references 5.
text.formatted: Organizing those parameters longitudinally, and reading them within the person, revealed an allostatic multisystem dynamic that is completely missed when laboratory results are read one by one, against population references <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref>.

text.text: Classical allostatic overload comprises energetic deficit (type 1) and social-conflict stress (type 2) 6 .
text.formatted: Classical allostatic overload comprises energetic deficit (type 1) and social-conflict stress (type 2) <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> .

text.text: Here we define a third: a biophysical overload and the conserved regime that counters it, in which HPCPh lower neural and systemic throughput, despite intact energy supply.

From an evolutionary standpoint, synaptic excitability did not emerge de novo for neural computation, but rather through the exaptation of ancestral osmoregulatory mechanisms originally evolved to counteract the Gibbs-Donnan equilibrium in primordial oceans: to prevent lethal osmotic swelling driven by impermeant intracellular polyanions, early cells established steep transmembrane ionic gradients; a critical failure there kills the cell in minutes [7] [8] [9].
text.formatted: From an evolutionary standpoint, synaptic excitability did not emerge de novo for neural computation, but rather through the exaptation of ancestral osmoregulatory mechanisms originally evolved to counteract the Gibbs-Donnan equilibrium in primordial oceans: to prevent lethal osmotic swelling driven by impermeant intracellular polyanions, early cells established steep transmembrane ionic gradients; a critical failure there kills the cell in minutes <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>.

text.text: Every action potential and every excitatory postsynaptic current admits Na⁺ and releases K⁺ at no immediate cost; the bill is paid afterwards by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, which consumes most of the signalling ATP of grey matter 10, 11 .
text.formatted: Every action potential and every excitatory postsynaptic current admits Na⁺ and releases K⁺ at no immediate cost; the bill is paid afterwards by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, which consumes most of the signalling ATP of grey matter <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> .

text.text: Hyperconnected microcircuits and sustained parallel firing in HPCPh can push the rate of Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ influx and of interstitial K⁺ accumulation beyond the maximal turnover of the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and the buffering capacity of astrocytes, approaching the threshold of spreading depolarization, first described in 1944 by the Brazilian neurophysiologist Aristides Leão [12] [13] [14] [15] .

text.text: What the organism then faces is a configuration that signals a concrete and immediate threat to the function of the CNS: a biophysical problem met first at the cellular level, by feed-forward programmes far older than vertebrates.
The membrane budget has been a non-negotiable condition of life since the first cells 16 .
text.formatted: The membrane budget has been a non-negotiable condition of life since the first cells <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16</ref> .

text.text: The compatibleosmolyte strategy that defends it is shared by bacteria, archaea and marine invertebrates 7, 17 .
text.formatted: The compatibleosmolyte strategy that defends it is shared by bacteria, archaea and marine invertebrates <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> .

text.text: An architecture with a narrow margin of trade-offs therefore lives with a permanent threat: one set not by primary mitochondrial failure, tissue hypoxia or substrate deprivation, but by the instantaneous kinetics of transmembrane transport and by the maximum rate at which extracellular K⁺ can be cleared per unit of time.
It is a matter of rate, not of fuel 18, 19.

text.text: The threat is always close by and depends directly on the processing load imposed by the environment.

Hence the central allostatic task, whose regulatory purpose is normally guided by stable patterns of systemic homeostasis (T4 and TSH; iron, ferritin and inflammation; glycaemia and insulin; osmolality and volume against vasopressin and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system), is displaced to guarantee the integrity of the central nervous system 20, 21 .

text.text: External performance is sacrificed to the defence of membrane viability (executive collapse, fatigue, fog, impaired memory, avoidance of novelty), peripheral feedback is subordinated to that defence, and throughput is lowered as a limit on information processing.
The water and ion axis is the primary line of that defence, but it is not the only one, because the source of the load is external, unpredictable and may not relent.

When the environment stays adverse, containment extends from the membrane to the set points that govern the whole organism: cortisol and the circadian rhythm, thyroid conversion, protein synthesis, iron handling, immune tone and the cellular memory of previous states are re-tuned, in a coordinated cascade, so that the central nervous system remains viable at the expense of everything else 22, 23 .

text.text: Read one value at a time, each of these shifts looks like a mild and separate abnormality, or passes as normal, and in practice they are often treated as independent failures of the gland or organ concerned, with strategies that often add to the very load the regime is trying to contain.

The serum osmolal gap is the difference between the osmolality measured by the laboratory, which is the real number, and the osmolality calculated from sodium, glucose and urea; it opens when particles that the calculation does not count are present in plasma 24 .

text.text: The osmolal gap is the most direct trace of the primary mechanism, but it certainly does not stand alone.
As the cases presented illustrate, it appears in the company of "all the rest": a multisystemic line of defence that is always on guard.
Five longitudinal adult series, offering different perspectives on the phenomenon, show its dynamics empirically.

The gap emerged from within-person longitudinal laboratory follow-up, but it was neither the first pattern we noticed nor the only one that can be made visible with the instruments of any clinical laboratory.

A finding typically seen only in severe ICU patients with multiple organ failure, in alcohol and other intoxications, in diabetic ketoacidosis, in renal failure and after osmotic infusions such as mannitol was chosen on purpose as the centre of this paper, written so that the findings could be translated immediately to any consulting room: not as a certainty, but as one more question, opening a window where none is easy to find 25, 26 .

text.text: The gap represents an effort the organism is making to survive, and illustrates its magnitude: an effort that is more often than not taken for granted or simply ignored.
It also illustrates one of the most primitive manoeuvres of the cell, one that allowed life to evolve and, in humans, to consciously experience it.

text.text: Concerning the osmolal gap, the reading depends on four routine instruments that answer four different physical questions 35, 36 (Fig. 1.1c): (1) a freezing-point osmometer measures the depression of the freezing point of plasma water, and so counts every dissolved particle, charged or not; (2) a direct ion- selective electrode measures the activity of free Na⁺ only; it is blind to any uncharged particle and, being direct, is also immune to the plasma water-fraction artefacts that affect indirect (diluted) electrodes 37 ; (3) a reagent strip for urine specific gravity reads a colour change driven by ionic strength; it sees ions and nothing else 38, 39 , which is why a dilute-looking strip can coexist with a cryoscopic urine osmolality that is not dilute at all; (4) a haematology analyser sizes red cells after re-equilibration in an isotonic diluent, so the mean cell volume reports the cell's intrinsic water content rather than the osmolality of the plasma it came from 40, 41, 42.

text.text: This series, and the model that emerged from describing what was happening and the physiology that plausibly explains the pattern, came from the very real effort of treating patients who had been resistant to standard protocols.
Establishing methods that any clinician could use to assist their patients was therefore always a goal.
The haematocrit-haemoglobin index, with zero as the line that matters, and the two Rules of Three were born from that effort.

The Ht -3×Hb index is an example of a strategy that can be used in any clinical setting with one of the most common laboratory tests, the blood count, as a proxy for the state of intercompartmental water distribution.

Haemoglobin is measured as mass per volume of blood; haematocrit is the volume occupied by the red cells after the analyser has re-equilibrated them in an isotonic diluent; their ratio is the mean corpuscular haemoglobin concentration (MCHC).
At an MCHC of 33.3 g/dL, haematocrit equals three times haemoglobin, so haematocrit minus three times haemoglobin is zero 43 .
text.formatted: At an MCHC of 33.3 g/dL, haematocrit equals three times haemoglobin, so haematocrit minus three times haemoglobin is zero <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">43</ref> .

text.text: A positive value means more cell volume per gram of haemoglobin: red cells carrying more water.
A negative value means denser, thinner cells.

Because the diluent is isotonic, the water the analyser reports is the cell's own, set by the solutes the cell holds and by its own volume regulation, not by the osmolality of the plasma at the moment of the draw.
The two Rules of Three.
The laboratory measures the osmolality of serum directly, by freezing it, and can also calculate what it should be from sodium, glucose and urea.
The difference is the gap: particles the calculation does not know about.

When those particles are present, even when the measured osmolality stays within or close to the population reference, the sodium value is no longer what would be needed to account for it, because other particles are represented in the measured osmolality.

Two Rules of Three show this immediately: (1) the first asks what the measured osmolality would be if the calculated value sat at 290 mOsm/kg; (2) the second asks where sodium would be if the measured osmolality were 290 mOsm/kg within that column.

text.text: • Serum osmolal gap = measured serum osmolality (OsmP) -OsmCalc.

Where glucose or urea was not ordered in that draw, an estimated gap = OsmP -2 × Na + -k is given and marked e, where k is the person's own longitudinal median (glucose/18 + urea/6) across complete draws (Patient 1, k = 9.6; Patient 2, k = 9.1; Patient 3, k = 13.1; Patient 4, k = 11.7; Patient 5, k = 8.9 mOsm/kg).

• First Rule of Three on measured serum osmolality (OsmP@290) = 290 × OsmP ÷ OsmCalc (or 290 × OsmP ÷ [2 × Na + + k] when estimated, marked e), which answers what the osmometer would read if calculated ionic osmolality sat at 290 mOsm/kg.
• Second Rule of Three, on sodium (Na@290) = 290 × Na⁺ ÷ OsmP along the measured route, and 290 × Na⁺ ÷ OsmCalc along the calculated route.
The measured route projects sodium onto the number the osmometer read: it keeps the proportion between sodium and all the particles counted, so it falls when uncounted particles are present.
The calculated route projects sodium onto an osmolality built from sodium itself, so it stays near 140 mEq/L whatever the gap: it is the control.
The difference between the two routes is the share of the measured osmolality that sodium does not account for.

• Yielded sodium = 2 × (140 -Na@290, measured route), which expresses in mOsm/kg, counting Na + with its accompanying anion, how far Na@290 by the measured route falls below 140; it equals the serum osmolal gap exactly when OsmP is 290 mOsm/kg and glucose/18 + urea/6 is 10 mOsm/kg.
• Urine-to-serum phase ratio = measured urine osmolality ÷ OsmP of the same collection (<1.0, free water released; ~1.5, equilibrium; ≥2.0, water held under vasopressin command) 46.

The configurations described across the cases are possibilities, not rules: the direction of a column is always read from the system as a whole, within the person, and in relation to the columns that precede it.

The background matters: the same movement reads differently depending on how pervasive and how long the containment has been, and entries and exits happen in steps, some changes being characteristic of one step and not of another.
The iron trio (ferritin, serum iron and transferrin saturation) is one example: it has several possible combinations, not a single pattern.

Absorption may be braked at entry; ferritin may be retained as a vault without inflammation; iron may be allowed back into the system and used as the brakes allow; and, once absorption returns, ferritin may take on a finer regulatory role.

With the same equation in consecutive hospital patients, the serum osmolal gap is centred at -2 ± 6 mOsm/kg 48 , and its within-person biological variation in healthy fasting adults is small 49 ; a gap ≥ 10 mOsm/kg lies at the upper boundary of the 95% reference interval and serves as our transition mark.

text.text: The gap measures the fluidity of the fast axis, that is, that uncharged solutes are crossing compartments.
It does not say in which direction the organism is travelling.
Direction is read from the slower buffers that the fast axis serves.
Entry is the column settling: water held (ratio ≥ 2), axes suppressed, iron braked, insulin quiet.

Reconstruction is the column releasing: water let go or natriuresis, axes returning, iron allowed back into the system and used as the brakes allow, IGF-1 rising when the person is recovering from longer anti-anabolic states, monocytes waking if they had been suppressed under prolonged overload, working insulin, a warm but non-inflammatory hs-CRP.
The gap says that the column is moving; the column, and its relation to the columns that precede it, says where.

Day 0 (peak of uncontrollable load): hs-CRP 6.1 mg/L (flagged and not read as cold containment).

The panel captured acute dual iron braking: Sat plunged to 11% and serum iron to 32 µg/dL with ferritin 98 ng/mL and ACTH 3.0 pg/mL, while the salivary cortisol awakening response three days later surged to 1.334 µg/dL.
After ten days away from the load (day 10), iron-entry blockade reversed: Sat rebounded to 42%, iron to 124, DHEA-S to 298 µg/dL, ACTH to 9.0 and hs-CRP to 0.80 mg/L.

Ten days after the load resumed (day 20), a multisystem reconfiguration emerged, following a pattern compatible with a feed-forward vasopressin urine lock (ratio 2.51; OsmU 721; urinary Na + 177), while the plasma gap stayed closed (1.9e; OsmP@290 291.9e).
On day 96, the system sat near equilibrium (ratio 1.92; gap 3.9e; OsmP@290 293.9e; cortisol 16.8 µg/dL).

On day 133, with contextual exit blocked, a "biological helplessness switch" pattern was documented live: morning cortisol dropped to 0.6 µg/dL with uncompensated ACTH (5.0 pg/mL) and five of six salivary cortisol points two days later fell below 0.05 µg/dL (Fig. 2d) 61 .

The parallel with Seligman's learned helplessness model 59 supports the perception of a shift from the readiness to fight and change the context (the attempts to escape the shock cage in the original experiments of the 1970s) to the point where the organism's internal prediction seems to switch off the main drive and take the opposite path, withdrawing inwards, at the edge of risk to the central nervous system under acute, intense or prolonged overload, especially without escape or consistent interpersonal support 62 .

text.text: The window between the startle response and radical shutdown may be very narrow in HPCPh, depending on the mismatch between the subject's architecture and the context.

This point carries profound clinical relevance and should be a goal of further research as soon as possible: forcing the patient against the CNS threshold could worsen the scenario, and many strategies that work in other phenotypes could fail here or make things worse.

• At day 59, urinary concentration peaked (OsmU 916, SG 1.028, ratio 3.27) with a negative gap (-6.7; OsmP@290 283.2), prolactin braking (35.8 ng/mL) and HbA1c 4.6%.

• By day 143, Na + shifted to 136 as urine diluted (OsmU 652, ratio 2.26), opening a +5.6 gap unmasked by OsmP@290 jumping to 295.8 (raw OsmP 288; Ht-3×Hb -1.1) as IGF-1 surged to 287 ng/mL and dysautonomia symptoms diminished significantly, alongside cognitive improvement, leading to a consistent functional gain.

Across all 5 cases, as we have been observing systematically in HPCPh, the line that always converges crosses the common ground that led us to organize the data in the first place: an intense, rapid and atypical biological response to changes in the nature or intensity of informational load, and the regression of symptoms and laboratory parameters when the external context was adjusted to each patient's architecture.
Organizing those parameters longitudinally, and reading them within the person, made the Third Allostatic Load evident to us.
The strategies to unveil it, such as the Rules of Three and the Ht -3×Hb index, were developed to make it visible in an easy way that can reach people who could benefit from the perspective (Fig. 6).

text.text: Five patients, opposite trajectories, one invariant biophysics.

Whether leaving prolonged containment in steps (Patient 1), entering a biological configuration named here "acute helplessness" under inescapable load (Patient 2), decompressing via the endothelial-natriuretic arm (Patient 3), resolving executive arrest in 4.6 months (Patient 4) or unlocking chronic peripheral-matrix dysautonomia (Patient 5), the systematically observed pattern draws one trajectory: the osmolal gap opened whenever uncharged solutes crossed the extracellular space and closed in held states, while the Rule of Three (OsmP@290 and Na@290) and the vertical column resolve magnitude and direction 16.

text.text: All five cases showed major biological turns in response to changes of context that consistently altered the load pressing on the individual architecture, without any pharmacological intervention or structural disease that could offer an alternative explanation.

That is what we propose as the Third Allostasis: the pervasive and costly effort, paid at the cell membrane, that HPCPh make to sustain the function of the central nervous system against adverse environmental patterns 11, 75 .

text.text: By showing these mechanisms we hope not to provide definitive answers but to raise many questions.
We have treated some of these patients for decades and never saw the pattern until a convergence of inexplicable findings and many inconclusive consultations made it progressively visible.
It means years of providing the best care we could, and yet not what the patient needed and deserved.
But then we did not know.
And that is a fact.

text.text: Recognizing the Third Allostasis through four routine instruments, the Rule of Three (OsmP@290 and Na@290) and whole-column reading may replace fragmented organ diagnoses and iatrogenic counter-measures, focusing the lens where it belongs: on the whole organism, on the relation between its systems and on their adaptive dynamics when the problem is the third allostatic load.
It then becomes possible to work on stabilizing what is really pushing the patient's systems towards shutdown, which may free the potential for a healthier and well-deserved life.
